analysis.one_liner: Makes critical habitat designations optional and adds extra scientific review before endangered species listings.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2003 with 8 Republican cosponsors, the bill died in the House Resources Committee without a hearing or a vote before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite key parts of the Endangered Species Act. Under current law, when a species is listed as endangered or threatened, the Interior Secretary must designate its "critical habitat" — the land the species needs to survive, where federal projects face extra review. This bill would make that designation optional, raise the scientific bar for listing species, require three-person peer review before major decisions become final, and give states, landowners, and permit applicants a bigger role. It was referred to the House Resources Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Real estate developers, timber, mining, and energy companies, and other large landowners. Critical habitat designations today happen automatically with every listing and trigger extra federal review of projects affecting the land; making them optional would spare landowners that layer unless the administration of the day chose to impose it. Stricter listing criteria, mandatory peer review, and guaranteed access to the government's draft wildlife analyses for permit applicants would further slow or soften restrictions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Developers, timber and mining firms, large landowners

how_it_helps.text: Changes the Interior Secretary's critical habitat authority from mandatory to discretionary, so no designation would be legally required when a species is listed.
Requires agencies to give greater weight to empirical, field-tested, or peer-reviewed data and to write new criteria that scientific studies must meet before a species can be listed.
Requires listing decisions to rest on field-observed data and directs agencies to accept and include landowners' own observations of species on their property in the listing record.
Bars any listing, delisting, recovery plan, or jeopardy finding from becoming final until three independently appointed scientific reviewers report on the underlying data.

Gives anyone seeking a federal permit or funding the right to see and comment on draft biological opinions before they are finalized, and requires agencies to explain when applicant-proposed alternatives are rejected.

analysis.who_pays: Endangered and threatened species would depend on the administration's willingness rather than a legal duty to protect their habitat, and the public would lose the clearest legal lever for compelling habitat protection. Agencies and taxpayers would also absorb the cost of the new peer-review, data-gathering, and applicant-participation requirements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Endangered species and the conserving public

drawbacks.text: The amendment replaces 'shall' with 'may' in the critical habitat provision, so courts could no longer force a designation an administration chose not to make — removing the enforceable deadline conservation groups rely on.

Listings could only rest on field-observed data and studies meeting criteria written after enactment, adding delay for rare or hard-to-survey species where waiting for more field data means further decline.

Every listing, delisting, recovery plan, and jeopardy determination would stall until three randomly appointed reviewers reported — up to three months per action, at agency expense — an honest cost even supporters would have to weigh against the review's value.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's peer review, transparency, and state-input provisions are reasonable process ideas that could improve the quality of species decisions. But its central change — making critical habitat optional — removes the one automatic, enforceable habitat protection in the law and replaces it with the judgment of whichever administration is in office. The benefits flow mainly to landowners and resource industries facing land-use restrictions, while the risk falls on species and the public's conservation interest. On balance, the costs outweigh the procedural gains.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Resources Committee in June 2003, sat there without a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote, and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Butch Otter introduced the bill on June 25, 2003, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Resources.
The CRS summary states the bill changes the Interior Secretary's power to designate critical habitat from mandatory to discretionary.

The bill would also weight field-tested and peer-reviewed data more heavily, set criteria for listing studies, require field-observed data and landowner input, mandate three-person peer review before major decisions, and give states and permit applicants a larger role in consultations.
The bill drew 8 cosponsors, all Republicans.

The last recorded action was a request for executive comment from the Interior Department on July 1, 2003; the bill never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote and expired when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The rules the bill wanted to change stayed on the books: mandatory habitat designation, existing listing standards, and consultation procedures were untouched. Landowners and resource industries seeking relief from habitat restrictions got nothing, and the public's existing conservation safeguards were preserved by the bill's failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing habitat protections and conservation rules

for.name: Rep. C. L. (Butch) Otter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 25, 2003 to make critical habitat designation discretionary and add 'sound science' requirements to Endangered Species Act decisions.

for.name: 8 of 229 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

against.name: House Committee on Resources
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Chair: Rep. Richard Pombo, R-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 25, 2003, requested executive comment from Interior on July 1, and then took no action; the bill was never reported out.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; the record shows no committee report, rule, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Every backer was Republican — the sponsor and all 8 cosponsors — and Republicans controlled the House and its Resources Committee, yet the bill still died in committee without a vote.

industries.note: Under current law critical habitat must be designated whenever a species is listed, triggering extra federal review of projects touching that land. Making designation optional would spare developers and permittees that automatic layer, at the cost of weaker habitat protection for species.

industries.industry: Timber, mining, and oil and gas
industries.note: Listings and critical habitat designations constrain extraction and access on public and private land. Discretionary designation, stricter listing criteria, and mandatory peer review would make restrictions slower and harder to impose.

The bill would spare ranchers automatic habitat designations and require agencies to include landowners' own species observations in the listing record. The data provision cuts both ways — landowner reports could also document a species' decline — but the main effect is a lighter regulatory load.
Groups that use critical habitat lawsuits to compel habitat protection would lose their main enforcement lever if designation became optional and field-data and peer-review hurdles slowed listings.
